method: Opened the exact primary sources with web.run; checked named sections. Teaching identities, policies and numbers remain this chapter's assumptions.

sources.sections: Printed pp.2–3 Bounded Context/Ubiquitous Language, p.13 Domain Events, p.16 Aggregates, p.36 Published Language
sources.supports: A model applies within an explicit context; domain events represent domain occurrences; a root enforces aggregate invariants; Published Language provides shared translation vocabulary.
sources.doesNotSupport: Our Order/Pay policy, transaction exception, event fields and numeric assumptions are examples, not Evans's prescribed implementation.

sources.sections: PDF p.2 versioned persistence example; true invariants and small aggregates throughout
sources.supports: Persisted versions reject a stale client's change; avoid giant graphs and clusters that fail to protect true invariants.
sources.doesNotSupport: Java object methods alone do not implement durable optimistic concurrency.

sources.sections: PDF pp.1–2 identity references/read composition, pp.4–5 Reasons To Break the Rules
sources.supports: Reference external aggregates by identity. Composing a read view does not license writes across aggregates. Deliberate multi-aggregate transaction exceptions need explicit reasons.
sources.doesNotSupport: The local Order/Stock reservation contract is our engineering choice.

sources.sections: Different vocabularies, unified models and explicit context relationships
sources.supports: The same domain term can have different models and meanings across bounded contexts; integration requires explicit mapping.
Persist the publication intent with the business update; a relay sends it later. A crash after publication but before marking can cause duplicate publication.
sources.doesNotSupport: Our demo does not run a relay/broker or validate end-to-end delivery liveness.

sources.supports: The message identity insert belongs in the database transaction containing business changes; acknowledge after the local transaction.
Row locks block conflicting writers until transaction end. Consistent lock acquisition order reduces deadlocks; an aborted transaction can be retried.
sources.doesNotSupport: 10 ms occupancy and the resulting hot-row ceiling are explicit teaching assumptions, not PostgreSQL benchmarks.

sources.sections: 13.2.1 Read Committed update predicate re-evaluation, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; 13.2.2/13.2.3 retry aborted transactions
sources.supports: After a concurrent update commits, an UPDATE predicate is re-evaluated. DO NOTHING can encounter a concurrent conflict absent from its initial snapshot; a subsequent statement obtains a new snapshot at Read Committed. Known serialization aborts require retrying the transaction.
sources.doesNotSupport: SQLite writer serialization is not experimental verification of PostgreSQL MVCC or isolation.

sources.sections: Current API v1/v2 distinction and API v1 pruning/parameter checks
sources.supports: API v1 saves the first result after endpoint execution starts, compares parameters, permits pruning after at least 24 hours, and can create a new request when a pruned key is reused.
sources.correction: The original chapter omitted API v1. The current primary document distinguishes v2 retry behavior, so this chapter now explicitly scopes first-result/24-hour claims to API v1.
sources.doesNotSupport: No universal provider guarantee or automatic expiry of UNKNOWN.

sources.sections: Event ordering; Handle duplicate events; signature verification
sources.supports: Delivery order is not guaranteed. Events can repeat, and separate event objects can describe the same object/type. Verify webhook signatures against the raw request body.
sources.doesNotSupport: No PSP signature implementation or live Stripe calls were performed in this demo.

sources.supports: Event Sourcing retains application changes as an event sequence that can reconstruct states, unlike merely notifying consumers from an outbox.
